title: Studio Website
headline: Small studio. Close collaboration.
description: A studio website with selected work, service scope, and a practical inquiry guide.
context: Fictional Common Room Studio designs clear websites for independent businesses. Two designers work directly with the owner from the first conversation to handover. This edition shows a café, an archive, and a maker’s shop.

sections.title: Work that earns its place
sections.body: Greenhouse needed opening hours, a readable menu, and directions that guests could find on a phone. We reduced the launch scope to five pages and agreed who would maintain each one.

sections.title: How we work
sections.body: A short discovery session sets the audience and the boundaries. We share one direction with reasons, review real content together, and leave the owner with a documented update routine.

sections.title: Start a conversation
sections.body: Bring the business name, the pages you need, a target date, and what you can supply. For this fictional studio, a suitable first project has one decision maker and time for two review rounds.

questions: studio name, audience, selected projects and permissions, actual services, availability, contact destination

title: Personal Homepage
headline: A place for the things I’m making.
description: Introduce your work, current interests, and ways to connect in a personal homepage.
context: Alex is a fictional independent builder exploring calmer tools for small teams. This homepage brings together selected experiments, a short biography, and an up-to-date now section.

sections.title: A little background
sections.body: I work where product decisions meet useful documents. Recent projects have included a client handover, a community directory, and a set of private project pages. I prefer a small working example to a long speculative roadmap.

sections.title: Selected experiment
sections.body: The project notebook started as a single weekly page. A short decision log turned out to be more useful than another stream of status messages. The next experiment is a clearer handover between the owner and their Agent.

sections.title: Open to
sections.body: Thoughtful collaborations on documentation, small web tools, and independent products. Introduce the problem, the people it affects, and the kind of help you need. Replace this sample invitation with your real contact details.

questions: name, biography, current work, interests, work links, contact details and visibility

title: Consultant Profile
headline: Make the next product decision clearer.
description: Present a consultant’s expertise, engagement formats, and qualification questions.
context: Fictional consultant Robin helps small product teams turn an ambiguous brief into a decision they can test. Engagements have a defined question, a named reviewer, and a written handover.

sections.title: Experience with context
sections.body: Robin’s sample work covers onboarding, customer communication, and internal knowledge tools. This profile deliberately describes the work performed rather than inventing client logos, credentials, or performance claims.

sections.title: A useful first week
sections.body: Agree the question and the available evidence. Speak with the people closest to the work, review one real workflow, and separate immediate changes from assumptions that need a test.

sections.title: Check the fit
sections.body: This service suits a team that can name a decision owner and share relevant material. A request to replace an entire product strategy without access to customers needs a narrower first step.

questions: consultant credentials, verified experience, services, engagement duration, availability, qualification criteria

title: Product Launch Page
headline: One notebook for the next project.
description: Launch a product with a concrete preview, use cases, and meaningful FAQs.
context: Fieldnote is a fictional project notebook for small teams. This example demonstrates the product story and a preview of its core workflow; product capabilities and availability are illustrative.

sections.title: See the first project
sections.body: A café website starts with the five pages it needs. The weekly note identifies the missing menu copy. The decision log records why online ordering is outside the first release. Each piece links back to the same brief.

sections.title: Who it helps
sections.body: Teams with a few concurrent projects and a named owner for each one. A readable project record can help collaborators join the conversation without searching through a long message history.

sections.title: Before you join
sections.body: In a real launch, replace this section with verified availability, plan details, data handling, and a working sign-up destination. This sample has no sign-up form and makes no promise about a live service.

questions: product name, verified capabilities, audience, sample workflow, availability, pricing and sign-up destination

title: Event Landing Page
headline: An afternoon for useful ideas.
description: An event website with agenda, audience, access information, and session details.
context: The fictional Common Room gathering brings independent builders together for short demonstrations and practical conversations. The sample event runs from 13:00 to 17:00; venue and attendance arrangements must be confirmed before use.

sections.title: Come with a question
sections.body: Bring a project you can describe in two minutes, or a question you are actively working on. Finished work is welcome, but an honest account of an unfinished experiment is equally useful.

sections.title: A comfortable afternoon
sections.body: Allow space between sessions and provide seating throughout. Publish verified step-free access, restroom details, transport options, and a contact for access requests when the venue is confirmed.

sections.title: What happens next
sections.body: The host collects only the information needed to organize attendance. Replace this sample with a real booking link and clear cancellation terms before inviting people. No registration is collected by this page.

questions: event title, confirmed date and venue, agenda, speakers and permission, accessibility, booking link

title: Newsletter Landing Page
headline: A useful note, every other Friday.
description: Explain a newsletter’s editorial promise with a sample issue and clear subscription expectations.
context: Working Notes is a fictional newsletter about small products and practical documentation. Each issue follows one real question from a rough idea to something a reader can try.

sections.title: From the sample issue
sections.body: A handover is useful when the next person can act without asking what every file means. Try putting the owner, the last review date, and the next action above the document list.

sections.title: The editorial promise
sections.body: Expect one subject at a time, enough context to judge it, and examples that can be adapted. This sample does not claim a subscriber count, testimonials, or a publishing history.

sections.title: Subscription details
sections.body: Add a verified subscription destination, delivery cadence, sender name, and privacy information before launch. Explain how to unsubscribe. This static sample stores no email addresses.

questions: newsletter name, audience, editorial focus, cadence, sample issue, subscription and privacy destinations

title: Community Homepage
headline: Build together, at a human pace.
description: A community home with a welcoming path, recurring activities, and participation guidelines.
context: The fictional Side Project Circle is a small peer group for people building useful things outside their day jobs. Members choose a manageable next step and return to share what happened.
rows: A task you can do together

sections.title: Your first visit
sections.body: Read the participation guide, introduce the project in a few sentences, and choose a gathering that fits. Listening is participation; nobody needs a polished presentation to attend.

sections.title: How we look after the space
sections.body: Give feedback on the work, ask before sharing someone else’s material, and keep private conversations private. The organizer should publish a clear reporting route and explain how concerns are handled.

sections.title: Make room for newcomers
sections.body: A rotating host welcomes first-time participants and explains the format. Keep event information current and offer a written recap for people who cannot attend live.

questions: community purpose, membership expectations, organizers, event cadence, conduct policy, joining route

title: Service Directory
headline: Find the right kind of help.
description: A readable directory with service categories, selection criteria, and provider details.
context: This fictional directory helps independent businesses identify the kind of support they need before contacting a provider. The sample listings are invented and are not endorsements.

sections.title: Choose by the work
sections.body: Start with the outcome you need, your deadline, and the material already available. A provider’s specific scope is more useful than a broad label such as full service.

sections.title: Before an introduction
sections.body: Ask about availability, relevant examples, who will do the work, and how costs are agreed. Confirm the provider’s current details independently before making a purchase.

sections.title: Keeping the directory useful
sections.body: Assign an owner to each listing and record its last verification date. Remove unavailable providers and identify paid placements clearly if the real directory includes them.

questions: directory audience, real providers and consent, categories, inclusion criteria, verification dates, contact routes

title: Case Study Showcase
headline: From scattered notes to a usable handover.
description: Tell a project story through constraints, decisions, evidence, and the finished result.
context: This fictional case study follows a small studio preparing a client handover. The work focused on making the next owner’s responsibilities visible, rather than redesigning every document.

sections.title: The original difficulty
sections.body: The client received useful files but could not tell which ones were current. Several links referred to earlier drafts, and no single page explained who would update the website after launch.

sections.title: What changed
sections.body: The studio created an index with a purpose, owner, and status for each deliverable. A short maintenance routine sat beside the index. Old drafts stayed in an archive rather than appearing as equal alternatives.

sections.title: What the example can show
sections.body: The sample result is an organized handover with explicit responsibilities. A real case study should add verified before-and-after evidence, permission to name the client, and any limitations in the evaluation.

questions: project background, client permissions, role, constraints, key decisions, verified evidence and outcome

title: Client Onboarding Guide
headline: A clear first week together.
description: Welcome a client with owners, access requests, milestones, and a first-week checklist.
context: Common Room’s fictional café project begins with one decision maker and a shared brief. This guide explains what the client supplies, what the studio prepares, and when the first review happens.

sections.title: Working agreement
sections.body: Use one review thread for each deliverable and identify the person who consolidates feedback. Urgent issues go to the project lead; a new idea goes into the scope discussion before work begins.

sections.title: Access without confusion
sections.body: List the systems required and the minimum role needed in each. The client grants access through the system’s own invitation process. Keep passwords and recovery codes out of this guide.

sections.title: Ready for the first review
sections.body: The kickoff is complete when the goal, the five-page scope, the content owner, and the first review date are understood by both sides. Missing inputs become named actions rather than hidden assumptions.

questions: client and project, stakeholders, working channels, access needs, milestones, required inputs

title: Project Brief
headline: Agree what this project needs to do.
description: A project brief that connects the audience, problem, scope, and acceptance conditions.
context: The fictional Greenhouse café needs a website that answers common visitor questions on mobile. The first release covers location, opening hours, the menu, the story, and contact information.
rows: A first-time visitor on a phone
Find each in one clear path

sections.title: The problem to solve
sections.body: Customers currently ask for information that exists in several places. The site should make the essentials easy to find and simple for the owner to keep current.

sections.title: Acceptance conditions
sections.body: Use approved content, readable type, working links, and layouts that fit mobile screens. The owner should be able to explain the update process at handover. Record any unresolved item before launch.

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: Confirm seasonal hours, the menu source of truth, and the person responsible for updates. Do not fill missing business details with plausible-looking information; mark them for the owner to supply.

questions: problem, audience, desired outcome, scope exclusions, content sources, decision owner and acceptance criteria

title: Statement of Work
headline: Scope that both sides can review.
description: A discussion draft with deliverables, responsibilities, assumptions, and change handling.
context: This fictional statement of work covers the design and handover of a five-page café website. It is a planning example for review, with commercial and legal terms to be supplied by the contracting parties.

sections.title: Responsibilities
sections.body: The studio prepares the design and build. The client provides approved text, licensed images, and one consolidated response per review round. Delays to those inputs require the schedule to be revisited together.

sections.title: Change handling
sections.body: Write down the requested change, its reason, and its effect on time and cost. Work outside the agreed scope starts only after both parties accept the revised plan.

sections.title: Before agreement
sections.body: Replace all sample details, attach the agreed pricing and payment schedule, and have the parties review the terms appropriate to their jurisdiction. This example is not an executed contract.

questions: parties, deliverables, exclusions, responsibilities, acceptance process, commercial terms and review requirements

title: Account Plan
headline: Build the relationship around useful outcomes.
description: An account plan with stakeholder needs, opportunities, risks, and next conversations.
context: The fictional Greenhouse account is entering its first quarter after a website handover. The studio wants to support maintenance without assuming the client needs a larger project.

sections.title: Current position
sections.body: The first website is complete in this example. The immediate opportunity is a clear maintenance routine, not a speculative rebuild. Record the client’s stated priorities separately from the studio’s ideas.

sections.title: Relationship risks
sections.body: Updates may stop if responsibility is unclear. A seasonal menu change could expose an outdated page. Keep the next review date and the owner of each content area visible.

sections.title: Ninety-day focus
sections.body: Check the information once a month, review actual visitor questions, and discuss improvements only when there is evidence of a need. A real plan should include verified commercial history in the private version.

questions: account history, stakeholder roles, verified goals, current commitments, risks and next review

title: Meeting Follow-up
headline: The meeting ends. The next steps don’t.
description: Turn a discussion into decisions, owned actions, and a reviewed follow-up draft.
context: In this fictional café kickoff, the client and studio agreed the first-release scope and identified two missing inputs. These notes are a draft for participants to check before they are shared.

sections.title: Decisions made
sections.body: The first release has five pages. Online ordering remains outside scope. The café owner consolidates feedback, and the studio records any proposed scope change before starting it.

sections.title: Still open
sections.body: The final menu text and seasonal opening hours are not yet confirmed. Those inputs affect content review but do not change the agreed page structure at this point.

sections.title: Follow-up draft
sections.body: Thanks for the discussion. We agreed the five-page scope and a Friday outline review. Please check the action list and flag any owner or date that is incorrect. The menu text and seasonal hours remain the two inputs we need next.

questions: meeting date, participants, verified decisions, open questions, owners, dates and intended recipients

title: Service Comparison
headline: Choose the support the project actually needs.
description: Compare service packages by scope, responsibility, and fit rather than vague feature counts.
context: This fictional studio offers three engagement shapes. The comparison helps a client choose between a focused review, a guided sprint, and a complete website project. Prices are intentionally omitted until scope is known.
rows: One existing flow and written findings
A team ready to make its own changes
An unclear problem with a deadline
A business launching its first site

sections.title: Compare the responsibility
sections.body: In a review, the client implements the changes. A sprint produces a direction and supporting evidence. The website engagement includes implementation within a defined page scope.

sections.title: Questions before choosing
sections.body: Who can supply content? Who will approve the work? Is the deadline fixed? The answers can change the suitable engagement more than the number of features listed.

sections.title: A sensible recommendation
sections.body: For the café example, the website engagement fits because the owner needs a complete handover and has no internal build team. Revisit the recommendation if the client already has a reliable implementation partner.

questions: service options, exact inclusions, exclusions, client capabilities, timeline and pricing assumptions

title: Client Handover Guide
headline: Everything the next owner needs.
description: A handover guide with deliverable locations, maintenance responsibilities, and recovery steps.
context: This fictional handover covers Greenhouse’s five-page website. The owner receives approved files and a short routine for keeping business information current. The index below uses descriptive locations rather than live private links.

sections.title: The first walkthrough
sections.body: Open the home page on a phone and follow the paths to hours, the menu, and directions. Then use the update guide to identify where each item is maintained. Record anything the new owner cannot find.

sections.title: Monthly maintenance
sections.body: Check hours and menu information, test contact links, and review whether any images or copy have expired. Record the review date and the person who completed it.

sections.title: When something goes wrong
sections.body: Capture the affected page, the time, and what was expected. Contact the named support owner through the agreed channel. Keep a verified recovery procedure in the private handover; do not publish credentials.

questions: deliverables and locations, owners, maintenance tasks, support channel, recovery procedure and access transfer

title: Quarterly Client Review
headline: What changed this quarter?
description: Review delivered work, client feedback, unresolved issues, and the next quarter’s priorities.
context: The fictional café account has completed its first quarter of routine website maintenance. This review separates delivered work from proposed improvements and keeps the client’s decisions visible.
rows: Two of three monthly checks recorded
Keep proposed events page in backlog

sections.title: What the record supports
sections.body: The team delivered the recorded menu updates. One maintenance check lacks evidence, so it should not be counted as complete. The two directions questions suggest an issue worth investigating, not a proven site-wide problem.

sections.title: What the client needs to decide
sections.body: Confirm the winter content owner and whether the location page deserves a small improvement task. The events page is a separate proposal and should not be implied as already approved.

sections.title: Next-quarter agreement
sections.body: Continue the monthly check, keep updates within the agreed support scope, and review recurring visitor questions. Add verified commercial figures only in the private client version.

questions: quarter, delivered work, verified metrics, client feedback, unresolved issues and decisions requested

title: Partnership Proposal
headline: A small collaboration worth testing.
description: Propose a partnership with mutual value, a bounded pilot, and review conditions.
context: Common Room Studio and the fictional Side Project Circle are considering a joint workshop. The proposal starts with one session and a shared review rather than a long-term commitment.

sections.title: Why try it
sections.body: The studio can learn where independent builders get stuck, while the community receives a practical session on clearer project briefs. Neither side needs to promise leads, revenue, or a permanent relationship.

sections.title: Pilot boundaries
sections.body: Run one ninety-minute workshop for a small group. Agree how names, recordings, and participant material may be used before the event. Each partner retains ownership of its existing material.

sections.title: Continue only with evidence
sections.body: After the session, compare preparation time, participation, and feedback. Decide together whether to repeat, change, or stop. Any sponsorship or payment arrangement belongs in a separately reviewed agreement.

questions: partners, shared audience, mutual value, contributions, pilot scope, ownership and success criteria

title: Project Status Board
headline: Know which work needs attention.
description: A project board with owned work, clear status definitions, and actionable blockers.
context: This fictional studio snapshot covers four client workstreams at the Monday review. Status is manually maintained; the page represents one review point rather than a live project system.

sections.title: Needs attention
sections.body: The archive index is blocked by missing labels. Leo should identify the content owner and agree a date for a usable sample. The workshop pack needs a reviewer, not more unrequested production work.

sections.title: Status definitions
sections.body: In progress means an owner is actively working on the next deliverable. Needs input means a named dependency prevents progress. Ready for review means the acceptance material is available. Complete means the agreed check has passed.

sections.title: The next review
sections.body: Update each row from its source record before the weekly meeting. Archive completed work after handover, and keep blocked items visible until the dependency is resolved.

questions: workstreams, snapshot date, owners, status definitions, blockers, source records and next review

title: Team Capacity Snapshot
headline: Plan the week with room to finish.
description: Compare available hours and committed work, with explicit assumptions about capacity.
context: This fictional three-person team plans one week at a time. Available hours already exclude leave and recurring meetings. Committed hours are estimates for the named work, not a measure of individual performance.

sections.title: Read the spare capacity
sections.body: The team has 14 unallocated hours across 82 available hours. Sam has the largest buffer, but work should move only when the skills and handover cost make sense.

sections.title: Protect the assumptions
sections.body: Do not add a full working week on top of the available-hours figure. Leave and meetings have already been removed. Revisit commitments when a task grows or an unexpected support request arrives.

sections.title: A practical adjustment
sections.body: Keep Leo’s remaining two hours for review and interruptions. Ask Sam to prepare the workshop checklist if the handover is small. Confirm the change with both people before treating it as the new plan.

questions: planning period, people and consent, available hours, commitments, estimation method and reassignment constraints

title: Issue Triage Board
headline: Separate urgency from noise.
description: Triage issues with impact, reproducibility, ownership, and a next investigation step.
context: This fictional product review contains four reported issues. Severity reflects the effect on a user task; priority also considers how many people are affected and whether a workaround exists.

sections.title: Triage order
sections.body: Verify the broken menu link and incorrect contact address first because they prevent intended actions. The heading wrap and image description still need owners and acceptance checks.

sections.title: A useful issue record
sections.body: Record the page, device, expected result, actual result, and a minimal reproduction. Avoid including private account data in screenshots. Link the verified evidence in the private issue system.

sections.title: Close with a check
sections.body: An issue is resolved when the original task works in the affected context and a reviewer confirms the result. A code change alone is not evidence that the user’s problem has gone away.

questions: issue list, severity definitions, reproduction evidence, affected tasks, owners and review process

title: Operations Scorecard
headline: A short view of the work that keeps things running.
description: Track operational measures with definitions, thresholds, and named follow-up actions.
context: This fictional monthly scorecard uses manually recorded service operations. Each measure has a definition and an owner so the team can investigate a change without guessing what the number means.

sections.title: Where to act
sections.body: Assign the open request today and recover the missing maintenance record. Review the incomplete handover with its owner before adding a new process to the whole team.

sections.title: Definitions matter
sections.body: The response measure counts a substantive first response, not an automatic acknowledgement. A maintenance check counts only when its result and date are recorded.

sections.title: Review the target
sections.body: Targets in this example are planning choices, not industry benchmarks. Compare several periods before interpreting a small change as a trend, especially when the sample is small.

questions: reporting period, measures and denominators, targets, data sources, owners and follow-up actions

title: Inventory Snapshot
headline: Know what is on hand before ordering.
description: An inventory snapshot with counted stock, reorder points, and reconciliation notes.
context: The fictional workshop store counts consumables before each monthly event. Quantities below are sample units from a manual stocktake, with no live warehouse connection.

sections.title: Order decision
sections.body: Notebooks are below the chosen reorder point. Confirm next month’s attendance and the supplier’s pack size before placing an order. Pens, badges, and paper remain above their sample thresholds.

sections.title: Count with context
sections.body: Record damaged or reserved stock separately from usable stock. If two counts disagree, reconcile the shelf location and unit before adjusting the total.

sections.title: Keep the record current
sections.body: Name the person who completed the count and the time of the snapshot. A purchase or event after that time changes available stock and should trigger an update.

questions: items, stocktake date, units, usable quantities, reserved stock, reorder rules and suppliers

title: Service Health Report
headline: A status report with evidence behind it.
description: Report service health, incidents, and follow-up work without implying live monitoring.
context: This fictional service report summarizes a single review window. The status labels come from recorded checks; they are not live availability indicators or promises about the Claw Me service.

sections.title: Current concern
sections.body: Investigate the delayed download with the request time, file size, and a repeatable test. One observation does not establish a general outage, but it deserves a named follow-up.

sections.title: What passed means
sections.body: A passed check applies only to the task and time recorded. It does not prove continuous uptime, complete coverage, or the absence of problems in untested paths.

sections.title: Next communication
sections.body: Publish a new snapshot when the investigation produces a meaningful result. Record any incident separately with its timeline, impact, mitigation, and remaining work.

questions: service scope, review window, checks and evidence, incidents, status definitions, owners and communication cadence

title: Team Directory
headline: Find the person closest to the work.
description: A team directory organized by responsibility, working preferences, and escalation routes.
context: This fictional team directory helps a collaborator find the right owner without exposing private contact details. Names, roles, and availability are illustrative.

sections.title: Start with responsibility
sections.body: Ask the named owner about the work, and include enough context to avoid a guessing game. A page link, a concrete question, and a deadline usually make a request easier to answer.

sections.title: Availability is a guide
sections.body: The working windows are preferences rather than guarantees. In the real directory, let people review how they are described and decide which contact details are appropriate to share.

sections.title: When the owner is away
sections.body: Use the agreed backup route for urgent delivery questions. Routine requests can wait for the next working window. Keep an explicit backup for any responsibility that cannot pause.

questions: team members and consent, responsibilities, contact routes, working preferences, backup owners and visibility

title: Launch Readiness Checklist
headline: Release when the evidence is ready.
description: A launch checklist with gates, owners, evidence, and a visible hold decision.
context: The fictional café website is approaching a review date. This checklist records readiness to ask for launch approval; it does not authorize publication.

sections.title: Current decision: hold
sections.body: Two gates remain open. Complete the menu-link check and the handover walkthrough before asking the owner to approve launch. A target date does not replace those checks.

sections.title: What ready means
sections.body: The named owner has attached the evidence required for the gate. If content changes after review, reopen the affected checks instead of keeping an outdated ready label.

sections.title: The launch conversation
sections.body: Summarize completed checks, known limitations, the rollback owner, and the proposed timing. The user or authorized project owner makes the publication decision separately.

questions: release scope, required gates, evidence, owners, unresolved risks, rollback plan and launch authority

title: Decision Log
headline: Keep the reason beside the choice.
description: A searchable-by-page decision register with alternatives, owners, and review triggers.
context: This fictional project log records three choices for a café website. It preserves the reasoning available at the time, including conditions that would justify reopening a decision.
rows: Keep menu as readable page text

sections.title: D-01: a smaller first release
sections.body: The team chose a five-page site to answer visitor questions first. An ordering integration would add operational work that the café is not prepared to own in this example.

sections.title: D-02: content people can read
sections.body: Readable page text keeps menu information available without requiring a download. The owner must still maintain the source whenever dishes or prices change.

sections.title: D-03: coherent feedback
sections.body: One person consolidates comments so the studio receives a clear response. This does not prevent others from contributing; it identifies who resolves conflicting requests.

questions: decision records, dates, owners, alternatives considered, reasons, evidence and review triggers

title: Conference Trip Planner
headline: Get there prepared. Come back with useful notes.
description: Plan a conference trip around confirmed logistics, selected sessions, and follow-up time.
context: This fictional two-day conference trip is a planning example, not a current travel recommendation. Replace transport, venue, and accommodation details with verified bookings before relying on the plan.

sections.title: Choose fewer sessions
sections.body: Select the sessions that support a real learning question. Leave time to compare notes and meet people instead of treating every timetable gap as an obligation.

sections.title: Keep logistics together
sections.body: Record booking references only in the private version. Include venue access information, local time, transport alternatives, and a contact for travel changes after verifying each detail.

sections.title: After the trip
sections.body: Write the useful findings while they are fresh. Separate ideas worth testing from contacts to follow up with, and review any message before sending it.

questions: confirmed dates and bookings, venue, learning goals, session choices, access needs and follow-up plan

title: Team Offsite Plan
headline: Leave with decisions, not just notes.
description: An offsite agenda with outcomes, preparation, facilitation, and space for recovery.
context: This fictional one-day offsite gives a small team time to review its working habits and choose two improvements. The venue, catering, and access arrangements remain items for the organizer to confirm.

sections.title: Prepare lightly
sections.body: Ask each person for one example of work that flowed well and one that became difficult. Share the agenda early and allow written contributions for people who think better before a discussion.

sections.title: Facilitate the decision
sections.body: Describe the problem before proposing solutions. Give quieter participants time to contribute, record disagreement accurately, and make the decision rule clear.

sections.title: Follow through
sections.body: The offsite is complete when the experiments have owners, a small first step, and a review date. Keep the recap short enough that the team can return to it during ordinary work.

questions: team size, purpose, location, access and dietary needs, agenda, decision rules and follow-up owners

title: Event Run of Show
headline: Everyone knows the next cue.
description: A production schedule with cues, owners, dependencies, and contingency notes.
context: This fictional ninety-minute community workshop has one host, one facilitator, and one venue contact. The schedule is a working production document for the people delivering the session.

sections.title: Before doors open
sections.body: Walk the room, check the display from the back row, and confirm who can make a timing decision. Keep the contact sheet private and available to the delivery team.

sections.title: If a session runs late
sections.body: Protect the closing time and shorten discussion before removing the break or access buffer. The host communicates the change clearly rather than silently pushing every later cue.

sections.title: If equipment fails
sections.body: Continue with the printed exercise and verbal instructions. A useful workshop should still work when the display is unavailable. Record any incident that affects the next event.

questions: event timing, venue, cues, owners, equipment, contact sheet and contingency rules

title: Weekly Planner
headline: A week with a few clear commitments.
description: A weekly planner that balances focused work, appointments, and a realistic review.
context: This fictional independent builder plans around three priorities and leaves space for routine work. The planner is a snapshot to discuss and update, not an automatic calendar integration.

sections.title: Three priorities
sections.body: Finish the brief, review a working example, and hand over the agreed result. New work should be compared with those commitments before it is added to the week.

sections.title: A daily reset
sections.body: At the end of each day, record what actually moved and the next useful step. Carry unfinished work forward deliberately rather than copying an entire unchecked list.

sections.title: Friday review
sections.body: What was completed, what changed, and what should stop? Use the answers to plan the next week. The aim is a credible schedule, not a perfect record of busyness.

questions: week, priorities, fixed appointments, energy preferences, available time and review routine

title: Moving Checklist
headline: Make the handover day less surprising.
description: Organize a move by dependencies, owners, and checks before and after handover.
context: This fictional household move uses relative dates so the plan can be adapted to a confirmed handover day. Local requirements, service availability, and contract notice periods must be checked separately.

sections.title: Pack for the first evening
sections.body: Keep essential clothing, chargers, basic kitchen items, and important documents accessible. Decide who carries the essentials bag so it is not accidentally loaded with the last boxes.

sections.title: Coordinate the dependencies
sections.body: A confirmed key handover comes before booking a tightly timed delivery. Record the owner and contact route for each arrangement in the private plan.

sections.title: Close the old place
sections.body: Use the agreed handover checklist and retain the records appropriate to your arrangement. Replace this example with the requirements of the actual tenancy, purchase, and service contracts.

questions: move date, locations, household needs, contracts, access arrangements, movers and service changes

title: Wedding Planning Brief
headline: Plan the celebration around what matters to you.
description: A wedding planning brief with priorities, responsibilities, guest assumptions, and open decisions.
context: This fictional small celebration has a working guest count of forty and a preference for a relaxed meal with close friends and family. All dates, costs, and supplier arrangements are illustrative.

sections.title: Three priorities
sections.body: Time with guests, comfortable access, and a meal that can be enjoyed without rushing. Use these priorities to judge optional additions rather than expanding the plan by default.

sections.title: Guest experience
sections.body: Confirm dietary and access needs through an appropriate private channel. Provide verified travel information and a clear schedule once the venue is booked.

sections.title: Open decisions
sections.body: Agree the budget range, booking deadlines, and who can approve a supplier. Keep personal guest information out of any public version of this page.

questions: couple preferences, guest count, confirmed date, budget, venue, access needs, responsibilities and supplier status

title: Travel Budget Worksheet
headline: Know the assumptions behind the trip cost.
description: A travel budget with checked totals, shared-cost assumptions, and a contingency line.
context: This fictional two-person, three-night trip uses illustrative EUR estimates. The figures are planning inputs, not current prices or booking recommendations.

sections.title: Working total
sections.body: The plan totals €900 for two people, or €450 each if all costs are split equally. A different sharing arrangement should be recorded explicitly rather than assumed.

sections.title: What is missing
sections.body: Check baggage, booking fees, insurance needs, and any activities before treating the estimate as complete. Record the source and date for each real price.

sections.title: When the plan changes
sections.body: Replace an estimate with the booked amount and keep the difference visible. Recalculate the total after every material change; do not hide overruns inside the contingency line.

questions: travelers, dates, currency, cost items, price sources, sharing arrangement and contingency

title: Road Trip Itinerary
headline: Leave room between the destinations.
description: A road trip itinerary with driving windows, rest stops, overnight plans, and alternatives.
context: This fictional three-day route is organized by relative travel windows rather than claiming current road times. Verify the actual route, local conditions, accommodation, and driver needs before departure.

sections.title: Build around the driver
sections.body: Set a driving plan that suits the actual drivers and conditions. Do not treat an estimated arrival time as a reason to skip breaks. Share responsibility for navigation and practical arrangements.

sections.title: A useful stop list
sections.body: Choose a primary rest stop and an alternative for each longer leg after checking that they are open and suitable. Keep booking and contact details in the private itinerary.

sections.title: If the weather changes
sections.body: Move the optional activity or shorten the day. The plan should make it easy to stop early and communicate a change, with accommodation and route alternatives verified in advance.

questions: route, dates, drivers, vehicle needs, verified journey times, accommodation, stops and alternatives

title: Project Kickoff Agenda
headline: Start with the decisions that unlock the work.
description: A kickoff agenda with preparation, timed discussions, outputs, and a closing check.
context: This fictional sixty-minute kickoff starts a five-page café website. The purpose is to confirm the goal, scope, responsibilities, and first review rather than solve every design question in one meeting.

sections.title: Before the meeting
sections.body: Share the draft brief and ask participants to bring current content and known constraints. Invite the decision maker, content owner, and delivery lead; a large audience is not required.

sections.title: During the discussion
sections.body: Keep unresolved questions visible. If a topic cannot be decided with the available evidence, give it an owner and a next step instead of forcing agreement.

sections.title: Close with a read-back
sections.body: Read the scope, exclusions, owners, and first review date aloud. Ask participants to correct the record, then prepare a follow-up draft for review before sending.

questions: project purpose, participants, decision authority, agenda duration, pre-reading and required outputs

title: Presentation Outline
headline: A proposal people can follow.
description: A four-part presentation connecting the problem, evidence, recommendation, and decision.
context: This fictional presentation proposes a clearer handover process for a small studio. Each slide has one job, with discussion notes available in the HTML and expanded in the PDF.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: New project owners receive files without a clear map. The team spends time answering where things are and which version is current. Start the presentation with one concrete example of that difficulty.

sections.title: The proposed change
sections.body: Create a short index with the purpose, owner, status, and next review date for each deliverable. Keep the existing files; improve the route into them.

sections.title: The decision requested
sections.body: Try the index on two handovers and review the receiving team’s questions. Agree an owner and a review date. Do not imply that the pilot has already been approved.

questions: audience, presentation purpose, evidence, recommendation, decision requested and speaker notes

title: Board Update
headline: The quarter’s choices, clearly presented.
description: A board-style update with operating evidence, risks, and explicit decisions requested.
context: This fictional small product team is reviewing a quarter of delivery work. Figures below are sample operating counts, not Claw Me company results or financial disclosures.

sections.title: Delivery and focus
sections.body: Ten milestones are recorded as complete. The two remaining items share a content dependency, so the team proposes resolving that dependency before expanding the scope.

sections.title: Risk and response
sections.body: A small team can become overcommitted when support work is invisible. Reserve capacity for known support needs and review any new initiative against existing obligations.

sections.title: Decisions requested
sections.body: Confirm the order of the two carry-over milestones and whether either new initiative should begin discovery. The board should receive verified financials separately where required.

questions: reporting period, governance audience, verified operating and financial evidence, risks and decisions

title: Annual Review
headline: A year of work, with the lessons attached.
description: An annual review organized around outcomes, evidence, lessons, and next-year priorities.
context: This fictional studio review summarizes a year of small client projects. It uses example counts to demonstrate a clear narrative without inventing revenue growth or customer endorsements.

sections.title: What the year produced
sections.body: The studio completed thirteen client engagements across three formats. Completion is a delivery count; it does not establish customer impact without follow-up evidence.

sections.title: What we learned
sections.body: Handovers benefited from a named maintenance owner and a short index. Projects with unclear content responsibility took longer to review. These observations should be checked against the actual project records.

sections.title: Next year’s focus
sections.body: Keep the useful handover practice, improve content preparation, and choose fewer internal experiments. Set a review method for those priorities before turning them into public claims.

questions: year, verified work inventory, outcomes, evidence, lessons, audience and next-year priorities

title: Experiment Results
headline: Show what the test can—and cannot—tell you.
description: Report an experiment with its hypothesis, sample, observations, and next decision.
context: In this fictional usability exercise, twelve participants tried two versions of a document index. The numbers illustrate reporting structure and are not a statistically validated product claim.

sections.title: Hypothesis and method
sections.body: An index with purpose and owner labels may help a new collaborator find the correct handover document. Each participant attempted the same lookup task using one assigned version.

sections.title: What we observed
sections.body: Five of six participants completed the task with the owned index, compared with four of six using the file list. The small sample and one-task design limit the conclusions.

sections.title: Next decision
sections.body: Keep the clearer labels for a broader trial and test with more varied tasks. Do not describe the difference as statistically significant or as proof of a general productivity gain.

questions: hypothesis, assignment method, sample, measures, observed results, limitations and next test

title: Customer Insight Report
headline: Keep the customer’s problem in view.
description: Present customer themes with traceable observations, exceptions, and product implications.
context: This fictional synthesis uses five example interviews about project handovers. The themes demonstrate a reporting format; they are not real customer statements or representative market research.

sections.title: The central difficulty
sections.body: Participants in the example could open the files but lacked context about their purpose and status. The difficulty was orientation, not file access alone.

sections.title: Preserve the exceptions
sections.body: One participant preferred a familiar folder structure and did not want another page to maintain. That view matters when considering whether the proposed index adds useful clarity or duplicate work.

sections.title: From insight to test
sections.body: Prototype a small index and observe a realistic handover task. Keep the original source references in the private research record and avoid turning paraphrases into attributed quotations.

questions: research sources, participant consent, sample, themes, exceptions, evidence references and implications

title: Postmortem Report
headline: Understand the failure. Improve the system.
description: A blameless incident report with impact, timeline, contributing factors, and tracked follow-ups.
context: This fictional incident concerns an outdated menu link during a café website update. Times and impact are sample values used to demonstrate a review structure.

sections.title: Impact and recovery
sections.body: The menu link was unavailable for a thirty-minute example window. The team restored the previous destination and verified it on mobile. The number of affected visitors is unknown and should remain unknown until evidence exists.

sections.title: Contributing factors
sections.body: The content checklist checked the visible menu label but did not test the destination after publication. The review process also lacked a named verifier for link changes.

sections.title: Follow-up work
sections.body: Add a destination check to the content routine and assign a verifier for the next update. Review the revised process after two changes; avoid a long action list without owners or due dates.

questions: incident scope, verified timeline, impact, recovery, contributing factors, owners and follow-up checks

title: Impact Report
headline: Connect the activity to the change you hoped for.
description: An impact report that separates participation, outcomes, evidence, and remaining uncertainty.
context: This fictional community program held three project-brief workshops. The report distinguishes attendance from learning and avoids claiming social or economic impact without supporting evidence.

sections.title: What was delivered
sections.body: Three workshops provided a practical exercise and a short written recap. Thirty-six attendances describe participation volume and may include repeat visitors.

sections.title: What the evidence suggests
sections.body: Twelve feedback respondents named a next step they intended to take. That is encouraging feedback, but it does not show whether the action happened or caused a lasting improvement.

sections.title: Improve the next report
sections.body: Ask for optional follow-up after a suitable interval and define what meaningful change would look like. Explain the response rate and preserve privacy when presenting examples.

questions: program purpose, activities, outcome definitions, data sources, response rates, limitations and follow-up

title: Executive Summary
headline: The essential decision in four pages.
description: Summarize a longer review with the recommendation, supporting evidence, risks, and action.
context: This fictional executive summary recommends a small handover pilot. It is designed to be read without the full working document, while keeping the important assumptions visible.
rows: An owned document index on two projects
One owner and a short review routine
Observed lookup tasks and receiver feedback

sections.title: Recommendation
sections.body: Run the bounded pilot before investing in a larger document-management change. The current evidence identifies a practical problem but does not justify a broad platform replacement.

sections.title: Reasons and tradeoffs
sections.body: The index can be created with existing material and reviewed quickly. It also creates a maintenance obligation, so its owner and update trigger must be part of the experiment.

sections.title: Action requested
sections.body: Approve the pilot scope, identify the two projects, and choose the review date. If the team cannot name a maintenance owner, resolve that gap before starting.

questions: source report, audience, recommendation, supporting evidence, risks, resource needs and decision

title: Product Demo Narrative
headline: Show the task, then the product.
description: A product demonstration narrative with realistic steps, success checks, and fallback notes.
context: This fictional demonstration follows an owner preparing a project handover with an Agent. The narrative is illustrative and should be aligned with the actual product’s verified capabilities before presentation.
rows: The Agent prepares a reviewable result
The next person has a clear starting point

sections.title: Begin with a real task
sections.body: Introduce the person, the project, and the difficulty in one minute. Avoid opening with a tour of every navigation item. The audience needs a reason to care about the next action.

sections.title: Demonstrate the boundary
sections.body: Show the draft and the owner’s review as separate moments. Use only capabilities that exist in the version being demonstrated, and identify sample data clearly.

sections.title: Keep a fallback
sections.body: Prepare screenshots of the same example in case the live environment is unavailable. Explain that the fallback is a recorded illustration rather than pretending the product is responding live.

questions: audience, verified product version, user task, demo steps, sample data, timing and fallback

title: Course Companion
headline: A place to connect the lesson to your work.
description: A course companion with learning outcomes, practice tasks, and reflection prompts.
context: This fictional short course teaches clearer project documentation. Each lesson ends with a small artifact the learner can compare with a worked example.
rows: A reader can name the goal
A reader finds the right file

sections.title: Practice: make the goal specific
sections.body: Rewrite “improve our documentation” as a concrete user task. For example: a new project owner can find the approved menu and identify who updates it.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.body: A useful index entry says “Approved menu — current café dishes and prices — maintained by the owner.” A filename alone rarely carries that much context.

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body: Which part of your own work is difficult for a newcomer to interpret? Write one change you can test this week and how you will know whether it helped.

questions: course subject, learner background, learning outcomes, lesson sequence, practice tasks and assessment

title: Study Schedule
headline: A study plan you can actually keep.
description: Plan focused study sessions, retrieval practice, and recovery time around a real deadline.
context: This fictional learner has four weeks to understand a new documentation workflow. The plan assumes three forty-five-minute sessions each week and one short review.

sections.title: A session structure
sections.body: Spend ten minutes recalling what you already know, twenty-five minutes on one task, and ten minutes checking the result. Adjust the timing to your own attention and access needs.

sections.title: When a session is missed
sections.body: Move the most useful task into the next available slot. Avoid doubling every later session; a smaller completed plan is more informative than an unrealistic recovery schedule.

sections.title: Check understanding
sections.body: Try explaining the concept without looking at the notes. If you can repeat the wording but cannot apply it to a different example, return to practice rather than collecting more material.

questions: subject, deadline, available time, current knowledge, session preferences and assessment goals

title: Reading Journal
headline: Keep the idea you might use later.
description: A reading journal for arguments, questions, connections, and a practical next experiment.
context: This fictional journal demonstrates how to record an idea without copying a source at length. The sample reading is an invented essay called “The Useful Handover,” not a published reference.
rows: Context makes files easier to use
When does an index duplicate work?
Onboarding has the same orientation problem

sections.title: Summarize in your own words
sections.body: Write the argument as you understand it and distinguish the author’s position from your response. Keep any quotation short, accurately attributed, and linked to its real source in the actual journal.

sections.title: Test the connection
sections.body: The useful connection is not simply that two subjects sound alike. Describe what would change in your work if the idea were true, and what observation might challenge it.

sections.title: Return to the entry
sections.body: At the next review, record whether you used the idea, changed your mind, or need better evidence. A journal becomes useful through retrieval, not through the number of entries.

questions: reading source, author, date, main argument, permitted quotations, questions and intended application

title: Habit Review
headline: Look for the conditions that help.
description: A reflective habit review with a modest record, context, and a next-week adjustment.
context: This fictional review tracks a short end-of-day planning habit. It is a personal reflection example, not medical or behavioral treatment advice.

sections.title: Notice the pattern
sections.body: The review happened on four of five days. The missed day followed a late meeting, while the shorter version helped on Thursday. Context is more useful here than judging the week as perfect or failed.

sections.title: Choose one adjustment
sections.body: Try a two-minute version on meeting-heavy days: record what moved and the next useful step. Keep the ordinary version for days with enough time.

sections.title: Review without punishment
sections.body: Ask whether the habit supports the work you care about. If it creates more pressure than value, change its scope or stop the experiment. The record is information, not a score of personal worth.

questions: habit, purpose, review period, observations, helpful conditions, obstacles and next adjustment

title: Career Development Plan
headline: Build evidence for the work you want to do.
description: A development plan linking a career direction to practice, feedback, and demonstrable work.
context: This fictional product designer wants to become stronger at research synthesis and facilitation. The plan focuses on work they can practice and review rather than promising a title or promotion.

sections.title: Choose a direction
sections.body: Describe the kind of responsibility you want, the work it involves, and why it matters to you. Separate your interests from assumptions about what your employer will reward.

sections.title: Make practice visible
sections.body: Create a small portfolio of working evidence: a synthesis, an agenda, and a decision brief. Remove private material and obtain permission before sharing work beyond its original audience.

sections.title: Review with someone
sections.body: Ask for specific feedback on the skill being practiced. A useful review identifies what improved, what remains difficult, and the next opportunity to practice in real work.

questions: career direction, current strengths, skills to develop, opportunities, support, constraints and review dates

title: Workshop Workbook
headline: Turn a vague project into a clear brief.
description: A printable workshop workbook with exercises, worked answers, and a closing action.
context: This fictional sixty-minute workshop helps a small team describe one project clearly. The HTML reveals worked answers after each exercise; the PDF includes them for facilitator review.

sections.title: Exercise: name the task
sections.body: Start with “A visitor needs to…” and finish with something observable. Worked answer: “A visitor needs to find today’s opening hours on a phone.” This is easier to test than “make the site engaging.”

sections.title: Exercise: set a boundary
sections.body: List the smallest useful result and one tempting addition to exclude. Worked answer: publish the menu and location; keep online ordering outside the first release.

sections.title: Exercise: choose the check
sections.body: Describe how another person will verify the result. Worked answer: ask a reader to find the hours and menu, record where they hesitate, and revise the unclear path.

questions: workshop topic, participants, duration, learning goals, exercises, worked examples and facilitation needs

title: Language Practice Guide
headline: Practice the conversation you are likely to have.
description: A language practice guide with a short scenario, phrase bank, and self-check prompts.
context: This fictional beginner Dutch practice focuses on ordering a drink in a café. It is a compact learning example with ordinary phrases and a suggested role-play.

sections.title: Try the exchange
sections.body: One person greets the customer and asks for the order. The learner orders a coffee, says thank you, and asks to pay. Repeat slowly before trying a natural pace.

sections.title: Change one detail
sections.body: Replace coffee with tea: “Een thee, alstublieft.” Keep the rest of the exchange familiar so you can focus on the changed phrase.

sections.title: Check what you can do
sections.body: Can you produce the phrase without reading it? Can you recognize it when someone else says it? Record the difficult part and ask a qualified speaker or teacher for pronunciation feedback.

questions: language, learner level, real scenario, phrases to practice, accessibility needs and feedback method

title: Personal Knowledge Index
headline: Find the note by what it helps you do.
description: Organize personal knowledge by purpose, status, and useful connections.
context: This fictional knowledge index belongs to an independent builder. It points to a small set of maintained notes rather than trying to categorize every saved link.
rows: Starting an ambiguous piece of work

sections.title: Start with use
sections.body: Give each note a title that hints at the task it supports. Add a short explanation of when to open it and a link to the real private note in your own version.

sections.title: Keep uncertainty visible
sections.body: Working notes can contain incomplete ideas. Mark them as such rather than presenting every saved statement as settled knowledge. Preserve source links and dates where they matter.

sections.title: A small maintenance routine
sections.body: At a monthly review, update the notes you actually used, archive obsolete ones, and connect any useful new material. An index should reduce retrieval effort rather than become another collection to manage.

questions: knowledge areas, existing notes, intended uses, status labels, source locations and maintenance routine

title: Goal Review
headline: Decide what deserves another month.
description: Review goals through evidence, obstacles, tradeoffs, and a deliberate continue/change/stop decision.
context: This fictional monthly review covers three goals for an independent builder. The record separates effort from outcome and makes room to stop work that no longer fits.

sections.title: What moved
sections.body: The handover example produced direct reader feedback, which is useful evidence of progress. The article goal exceeded the available writing time. The app experiment lacked a concrete need.

sections.title: What to change
sections.body: Choose one article based on the questions readers actually asked. Keep a small weekly writing slot and define a finished draft before adding a publication target.

sections.title: What to release
sections.body: Stopping the app experiment frees attention for work with a clearer purpose. Record why it stopped so the same idea does not return as an unexplained obligation next month.

questions: goals, review period, evidence, constraints, changed priorities and continue/change/stop decisions

title: Content Calendar
headline: Give every piece a reason to exist.
description: A content calendar with audience questions, formats, owners, and review status.
context: This fictional studio plans four weeks of content around questions from small-business clients. The calendar is an editorial plan; it does not schedule or publish posts.
rows: What belongs in a project brief?
How do I prepare website content?
When should I update a website?

sections.title: The editorial thread
sections.body: Each piece should help a prospective client prepare for useful work. Reuse the café example to connect the series, but give each article a distinct question and takeaway.

sections.title: Review before publication
sections.body: The owner checks accuracy, permissions, links, and the desired next action. A draft is not approved simply because its calendar date has arrived.

sections.title: Learn from the response
sections.body: Record meaningful questions and qualified inquiries rather than treating every impression as success. At the end of the month, decide which subject deserves a follow-up.

questions: audience, content goals, channels, dates, topics, owners, review workflow and measurement

title: SEO Content Brief
headline: Answer the reader’s question completely.
description: A search-focused content brief with intent, outline, evidence needs, and editorial checks.
context: This fictional brief plans an article about preparing content for a small-business website. It does not claim current search volumes, rankings, or competitor positions.

sections.title: Search intent
sections.body: The reader is likely preparing for a website project and needs practical inputs. The article should help them collect approved text, contact information, opening hours, and licensed images.

sections.title: Outline with substance
sections.body: Use a five-page café example to demonstrate the checklist. Explain how to mark missing information and why the content owner matters. Avoid repeating the target phrase where it adds no meaning.

sections.title: Editorial acceptance
sections.body: Check that the article answers the main question, cites real sources where claims need support, and uses descriptive headings. Add current keyword research only after it has been collected and verified.

questions: target reader, search question, current keyword research if available, outline, sources, internal links and acceptance checks

title: Launch Announcement
headline: A clearer way to hand over a project.
description: Draft a launch announcement with a concrete change, audience benefit, and verified next step.
context: This fictional announcement introduces a studio’s new handover guide. It is a message draft for review, not a sent email or published product claim.

Find the current files and their owners
A small handover improvement we tested

sections.title: The announcement draft
sections.body: We have put the project files, their purpose, and their update owners into one handover guide. Start with the index, open the item you need, and see who maintains it.

sections.title: Make the benefit concrete
sections.body: The change helps a receiving team orient itself. Describe that task directly instead of promising effortless collaboration or dramatic productivity gains without evidence.

sections.title: Before release
sections.body: Replace the sample destination with the approved page, confirm the availability statement, and have the owner review the message. Adapt the length to the channel without changing the underlying claim.

questions: what is launching, verified availability, audience, concrete benefit, channels, approved links and review owner

title: Audience Profile
headline: Understand the person making the decision.
description: An audience profile grounded in tasks, constraints, questions, and evidence gaps.
context: This fictional profile describes an independent café owner preparing a first website. It is a working hypothesis for research, not a demographic fact about all business owners.
rows: Make hours and menu easy to find
Who maintains the site after launch?

sections.title: The situation
sections.body: The owner is balancing the website project with daily operations. A useful service explains the required inputs and review moments in practical terms rather than expecting the owner to learn design terminology.

sections.title: Likely questions
sections.body: What do I need to supply? How many reviews are included? What happens when the menu changes? Treat these as questions to test in conversations, not quotations from a real customer.

sections.title: Evidence to collect
sections.body: Speak with relevant owners about a recent project decision. Record differences and exceptions, then update the profile. Avoid adding age, income, or personality traits that do not explain the task.

questions: audience task, context, constraints, decision process, source evidence, uncertainties and research plan

title: Messaging Guide
headline: Say the same useful thing, clearly.
description: A messaging guide with a core promise, supporting points, proof requirements, and examples.
context: This fictional studio’s message is about clear scope and useful handover. The guide helps collaborators describe the service consistently without claiming outcomes that have not been measured.
rows: A website your next owner can maintain
One feedback owner and two review rounds

sections.title: Lead with the task
sections.body: For an owner preparing a first website, explain what they receive and how the project proceeds. “A five-page website with an update guide” says more than “a transformative digital experience.”

sections.title: Adapt without drifting
sections.body: A short headline can emphasize the handover; a proposal can explain responsibilities and acceptance. Both should describe the same actual service.

sections.title: Claims to avoid
sections.body: Do not invent customer counts, awards, conversion improvements, or guaranteed results. When real evidence becomes available, attach its source and the conditions under which it was observed.

questions: brand, audience, actual offer, core message, supporting evidence, tone and prohibited claims

title: Channel Performance Report
headline: Compare the response, not just the reach.
description: Review channel activity with denominators, qualified outcomes, and attribution limits.
context: This fictional monthly campaign report uses sample channel counts. A qualified inquiry means a person described a relevant project and asked for a conversation. Attribution is last reported source in this example.

sections.title: Read the small sample
sections.body: The partner mention produced three qualified inquiries from forty visits, while search produced three from two hundred. The counts are small and the audiences differ, so this is a prompt for investigation rather than a stable ranking.

sections.title: Check the definition
sections.body: Use the same qualification rule across channels. Record how a source was assigned and how unknown sources are handled. A person may encounter several channels before inquiring.

sections.title: Next month’s test
sections.body: Repeat a useful partner example and improve the search landing page’s next step. Keep the measurement method unchanged long enough to compare the results meaningfully.

questions: period, channels, visits, outcome definitions, attribution method, costs if known and next tests

title: Referral Program Brief
headline: Make introductions easy to understand.
description: A referral program planning brief with eligibility, process, rewards, and review questions.
context: This fictional studio is considering a simple referral pilot. The program is not active; reward terms and local requirements need review before any offer is made.
rows: Ask the prospect before sharing details

sections.title: The pilot purpose
sections.body: Encourage relevant introductions from people who understand the studio’s work. A useful referral is a good fit for both sides, not simply a name added to a list.

sections.title: Terms to decide
sections.body: Define who can participate, which projects qualify, when a reward is earned, and what happens if work is cancelled. Keep the wording plain and have the actual terms reviewed before launch.

sections.title: Measure the quality
sections.body: Track relevant introductions, qualified conversations, and participant questions. Review whether the process creates confusion or pressure before expanding it.

questions: program purpose, participants, eligibility, proposed reward, milestone, consent process and reviewed terms

title: Customer Story
headline: The owner knew what to do next.
description: A customer story with a concrete problem, the work performed, and evidence-ready outcomes.
context: This fictional café story demonstrates a customer narrative without invented testimonials. Replace the example with approved customer material and verified results before publishing it as a real story.

sections.title: The customer’s situation
sections.body: The café owner had useful website files but was unsure which ones were current. The handover needed to support ordinary updates during a busy working week.

sections.title: The work together
sections.body: The studio and owner agreed the source of truth for each page, organized the deliverable index, and walked through a menu update. The owner reviewed the guide before handover.

sections.title: Evidence to add
sections.body: A real story should show what the customer actually experienced, with permission to use their name and words. Record the source of any outcome claim and describe the scope of the work honestly.

title: Brand Guidelines
headline: A recognizable voice across useful pages.
description: A compact brand guide with typography, color roles, writing examples, and usage checks.
context: This Claw Me example uses the shared Archivo and Bitter fonts, quiet surfaces, green actions, and coral brand accents. The guide is a practical companion to the bundled Tailwind source.

sections.title: Typography in use
sections.body: Use Archivo for operational labels and dense information. Use Bitter for document headings. Keep headings descriptive and avoid squeezing text with excessive letter spacing.

sections.title: Color with a purpose
sections.body: The green accent identifies a useful next action or active state. Status labels need words as well as color. White and quiet neutral surfaces keep long documents readable.

sections.title: Write like a colleague
sections.body: Prefer “Review the project brief” to “Unlock your project potential.” State what a control does and describe an outcome that the artifact can actually support. Keep implementation notes in source documentation.

questions: brand identity, existing tokens, fonts and licenses, voice, component roles, accessibility and examples

title: Cash Flow Snapshot
headline: See the timing behind the balance.

context: This fictional four-month EUR scenario demonstrates cash timing for a small studio. Expected receipts and payments are assumptions, not accounting records or financial advice.

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Each closing amount equals opening cash plus receipts minus payments. The next month starts with the previous closing amount. This example ends December at €4,500.

sections.title: The timing question
sections.body: October has the largest net outflow in the sample. Check when receipts are expected and which payments are committed before using the scenario to make a decision.

sections.title: Keep assumptions separate
sections.body: Replace expected amounts with verified records as they become available. A cash-flow view is not the same as profit, and it should not silently mix tax, credit, or personal funds.

title: Expense Review
headline: Review the spending with its purpose attached.
description: An expense review with categories, amounts, evidence, and questions for the owner.
context: This fictional monthly studio review contains four EUR expense categories. It is an organizational example; treatment for bookkeeping or tax should follow the actual records and applicable professional guidance.

sections.title: The monthly total
sections.body: The four categories total €760. Check that each transaction appears once and that refunds or credits are handled consistently before comparing the total with another month.

sections.title: Questions to resolve
sections.body: Confirm which software subscriptions are still used and whether the travel record has its supporting receipt. Missing evidence should remain visible rather than being replaced with an invented explanation.

sections.title: The next review
sections.body: Record the owner’s decision on recurring costs and any action to obtain missing documents. Keep personal or sensitive transaction details in the private version.

questions: period, currency, transactions, categories, supporting evidence, recurring costs and review owner

title: Pricing Comparison

context: This fictional comparison uses three invented software plans for a five-person team. The amounts are illustrative EUR monthly prices, not current vendor offers.

sections.title: Beyond the headline
sections.body: Compare required features, storage limits, billing commitments, support, export options, and any usage charges. A one-euro difference is not meaningful if an option cannot meet the actual requirement.

sections.title: Before a purchase
sections.body: Replace the sample plans with verified current quotes and record their dates, currency, and tax basis. Recalculate if the team size or billing term changes.

sections.title: Decision requested

title: Vendor Comparison

sections.title: A provisional shortlist

title: Invoice Summary

title: Renewal Tracker
