context: This fictional studio tracker shows four recurring services. Dates and amounts are illustrative; the real contract determines notice requirements and renewal behavior.

sections.title: Start with the agreement
sections.body: Record the actual notice period, renewal term, and cancellation route from the current contract. A reminder date should leave time to decide and complete the required process.

sections.title: Review the usefulness
sections.body: Ask whether the service is used, whether the plan fits, and whether any data needs to be exported before a change. Keep the current price and renewal quote separate.

sections.title: Record the decision
sections.body: Each owner marks renew, change, or end with a reason and evidence of the completed action. A planned cancellation is not a completed cancellation.

questions: services, current contracts, notice periods, renewal dates, owners, usage evidence and decisions

title: Financial Assumptions Sheet
headline: Make the model’s inputs easy to challenge.
description: Document scenario inputs, units, rationale, and the effect of changing assumptions.
context: This fictional studio planning model uses a simple monthly revenue scenario. It is a demonstration of assumption management, not a forecast of Claw Me or a recommendation about business finances.

sections.title: Base scenario
sections.body: Two projects at €2,400 produce €4,800 in modeled revenue. Subtracting €1,200 in direct project costs and €1,800 in fixed costs leaves €1,800 before items not included in this simplified model.

sections.title: One-project scenario
sections.body: At one project, modeled revenue is €2,400 and the same calculation leaves €0. This illustrates sensitivity to project volume; it is not a complete profit or cash-flow calculation.

sections.title: What remains outside
sections.body: Tax, timing, owner compensation, financing, and other relevant items are not modeled here. Add the actual inputs and have the model reviewed before relying on it for a material decision.

questions: model purpose, inputs, units, evidence, scenario ranges, exclusions and review requirements

title: Administration Checklist
headline: Close the month without losing the loose ends.
description: A monthly administration checklist with evidence, ownership, and unresolved items.
context: This fictional studio routine organizes records and recurring administrative work. It is a workflow example, not a statement of legal filing or tax obligations.

sections.title: Work from the source
sections.body: Use the actual invoice, agreement, or system record for each check. Keep an unresolved item open when evidence is missing rather than marking the task complete because time was spent on it.

sections.title: Handle private information carefully
sections.body: Store sensitive records in the appropriate private location and give access only to the people who need it. A public checklist can describe the process without exposing the underlying documents.

sections.title: End with a short exception list
sections.body: Record what remains, who owns it, and the next date to check. Confirm any formal obligations with the responsible professional or authority for the actual organization.

questions: organization, monthly tasks, source records, owners, deadlines, access needs and exception handling

title: Literature Review
headline: Compare the arguments before drawing a conclusion.
description: A literature review structure with source scope, claims, methods, and gaps.
context: This fictional review explores how document context affects handovers. The source records below are invented teaching examples, not real publications or citations. Replace them with verified literature in an actual review.

sections.title: Define the review question
sections.body: Ask which document features help a new owner find and maintain the right material. Set the context and inclusion criteria before collecting sources so the review does not become an unbounded reading list.

sections.title: Synthesize the disagreement
sections.body: The examples suggest that context can help retrieval while adding maintenance work. Compare the methods and settings behind those positions rather than counting how many sources appear to agree.

sections.title: Identify the gap
sections.body: A useful next study would observe both initial lookup and later maintenance. In the real review, preserve full citations, source links, search dates, and reasons for excluding material.

questions: research question, search scope, real source citations, inclusion criteria, methods, findings and gaps

title: Competitor Research
headline: Compare the alternatives a user would really consider.
description: A competitor research brief with verified observations, evaluation criteria, and unknowns.
context: This fictional comparison uses three invented approaches to project handover: a shared folder, a document index, and a project portal. It makes no claims about named commercial products.

sections.title: Start with the user’s choice
sections.body: A competitor is not always another branded tool. A familiar folder or a manual routine may be the real alternative, with lower setup effort and known limitations.

sections.title: Record observations precisely
sections.body: For a real product comparison, note the version, plan, date, and tested workflow. Keep marketing claims separate from behavior you actually observed.

sections.title: Draw a bounded conclusion
sections.body: The index offers explicit context with a modest setup in this example, but it creates a maintenance task. Test whether that tradeoff helps the actual receiving team before recommending a switch.

questions: user task, actual alternatives, evaluation criteria, verified sources and dates, observations and unknowns

title: Interview Synthesis
headline: Keep every theme connected to an observation.
description: Synthesize interviews into themes, counterexamples, and questions for the next round.
context: This fictional synthesis uses four invented participant records about receiving project files. No text is an attributed quotation from a real person.

Found the folder but not the first step

sections.title: Theme: context at the point of use
sections.body: Three example records concern information surrounding the file rather than the file itself. That suggests a prototype should test labels, ownership, and a clear entry point.

sections.title: Counterexample: another thing to maintain
sections.body: P04’s example raises a cost that the synthesis must preserve. A new index may be unwelcome if it duplicates an existing routine without making retrieval easier.

sections.title: Next research question
sections.body: Observe a handover task with a small index and ask the receiving person to maintain one item later. Keep participant consent, transcripts, and identifying information in the appropriate private research record.

questions: research question, participant consent, interview records, observations, themes, counterexamples and next questions

title: Survey Results
headline: Show the response behind the percentage.
description: A survey report with counts, denominators, question wording, and response limitations.
context: This fictional twenty-response survey asks which handover detail is most often missing. Respondents chose one answer, and the sample is illustrative rather than representative.

sections.title: The question asked
sections.body: “Which one detail is most often missing when you receive project files?” The single-choice format forces a priority and should not be interpreted as showing that other problems were absent.

sections.title: What the result says
sections.body: Fourteen of twenty example responses selected version or owner information. The report should show the counts beside percentages because each response changes the result by five percentage points.

sections.title: Limits and next step
sections.body: The recruitment method and population are not defined in this teaching example. In a real report, describe both and use follow-up conversations to understand what respondents meant by their choices.

questions: survey question wording, recruitment, sample size, raw counts, missing responses, limitations and next steps

title: Market Landscape
headline: Map the approaches before picking a position.
description: A market landscape organized by user needs, solution approaches, and evidence gaps.
context: This fictional landscape examines ways small teams organize project knowledge. It is a conceptual map, not a current estimate of market size, share, or vendor performance.

sections.title: Define the boundary
sections.body: The landscape concerns project knowledge for small teams, not every collaboration product. State what is inside and outside the analysis before comparing approaches.

sections.title: Look for unmet work
sections.body: A team may already store files successfully but struggle to transfer responsibility. Investigate that specific task rather than assuming the market needs another all-purpose workspace.

sections.title: Evidence needed
sections.body: For a real assessment, collect current product observations, customer behavior, and credible market sources. Separate known facts, estimates, and hypotheses in the final map.

questions: market boundary, user jobs, real alternatives, current sources, evidence gaps and positioning question

title: Dataset Guide
headline: Make the data understandable before analysis.
description: A dataset guide with field definitions, units, provenance, and quality checks.
context: This fictional dataset records handover tasks in a small usability exercise. The field examples describe a schema; they do not contain real participant information.

sections.title: Unit of observation
sections.body: One row represents one task attempt. A participant who performs several tasks may have several rows, so row count is not automatically participant count.

sections.title: Quality checks
sections.body: Require unique record identifiers, known variant values, nonnegative durations, and a consistent completion definition. Record missing values explicitly instead of substituting zero.

sections.title: Responsible reuse
sections.body: Keep identifying data out of the analysis extract. Document collection dates, consent, transformations, and permitted uses in the actual dataset record before sharing it.

questions: dataset purpose, source, unit of observation, schema, units, missing values, transformations and permitted use

title: Evidence Tracker
headline: See which claim still needs support.
description: Track claims against source quality, verification state, and next research actions.
context: This fictional evidence register supports a handover improvement proposal. The entries are sample research tasks, not proof that the claims are true.
rows: Owners struggle to identify current files

sections.title: Keep the claim narrow
sections.body: “An index helps this team find approved files” is easier to evaluate than “indexes improve productivity.” Match the evidence to the actual scope of the claim.

sections.title: Assess the source
sections.body: Record where the evidence came from, when it was collected, and what could make it misleading. A persuasive quotation does not replace a relevant method or representative sample.

sections.title: Use the gaps
sections.body: The untested maintenance claim is important because the proposed change creates ongoing work. Prioritize that check before presenting the index as a durable solution.

questions: claims, evidence standards, real source records, verification status, limitations, owners and next actions

title: Technology Assessment
headline: Evaluate the fit against the actual workload.
description: A technology assessment with requirements, observed behavior, risks, and a bounded trial.
context: This fictional assessment compares a static document site, a wiki, and a custom application for a team handover library. It describes approaches without claiming current library or vendor capabilities.

sections.title: Start with requirements
sections.body: The team needs readable reference pages and occasional updates. It has not established a need for custom operational actions, so those should not dominate the first decision.

sections.title: Risk to examine
sections.body: A custom application can create a larger maintenance obligation than the content problem warrants. A wiki may fit editing needs but still requires ownership and review conventions.

sections.title: Trial recommendation
sections.body: Test the smallest approach against two real handovers. Verify current capabilities and security requirements from primary documentation before selecting an actual product or technical stack.

questions: workload, requirements, actual candidates and versions, verified documentation, operational ownership and trial criteria

title: Research Plan
headline: A study small enough to answer one question.
description: Plan research with a clear question, participant criteria, method, and decision use.
context: This fictional study asks whether a document index helps a new project owner find the approved material. It is a planning example with a small exploratory sample.

sections.title: The research question
sections.body: Can a person unfamiliar with the project find the approved menu and identify its update owner? Keep the task stable enough that observations can be compared.

sections.title: Method and care
sections.body: Explain the purpose, obtain consent, and let participants stop. Observe behavior without coaching toward the answer. Store any recordings or identifying notes only where the participant agreement permits.

sections.title: Decision use
sections.body: The study can identify usability problems and suggest revisions. Six exploratory sessions do not establish a population-wide effect. Decide in advance what evidence would justify another iteration.

questions: research question, decision to inform, participant criteria, consent, method, task, analysis and limits

title: Product Requirements
headline: Describe the user outcome before the feature list.
description: A product requirements document with scope, user tasks, acceptance criteria, and open decisions.
context: This fictional feature gives a project owner a maintained handover index. The specification describes desired behavior for review and does not claim that the feature is already implemented.

Date is visible in the index

sections.title: User problem
sections.body: A receiving collaborator can open the project folder but cannot tell which item is current or who maintains it. The feature should help them complete that orientation task.

sections.title: Scope boundaries
sections.body: The first version organizes references and responsibility. It does not add a new file editor, automatic synchronization, or a permission system of its own.

sections.title: Open decisions
sections.body: Confirm who may approve an entry, how archived items appear, and what happens when a referenced file is removed. Resolve these behaviors before implementation begins.

questions: user problem, audience, desired behavior, scope, acceptance criteria, dependencies and open decisions

title: Feature Specification
headline: Make the edge cases part of the design.
description: Specify a feature through states, transitions, validation, and recovery behavior.
context: This fictional specification covers approving a handover entry. Approval means the owner has reviewed the reference and its context; it does not automatically change file sharing.

sections.title: Main flow
sections.body: The author supplies a title, purpose, reference, and update owner. The reviewer checks the content and either approves it or returns it with a concrete reason.

sections.title: Validation and recovery
sections.body: A missing reference prevents submission and should be explained beside the field. If the reference becomes unavailable after approval, show that condition and preserve the entry for repair.

sections.title: Permission boundary
sections.body: Approval is a content state, not authorization to publish or grant access. The implementation must use the actual platform’s permission model and make any separate sharing action explicit.

questions: feature behavior, user roles, states, transitions, validation rules, permissions and recovery cases

title: API Documentation
headline: A small API example with a complete contract.
description: Document an illustrative API through resources, fields, responses, and error handling.
context: This fictional API describes a handover-entry resource for a proposed application. The route and payload are examples only; they are not a live Claw Me endpoint.

sections.title: Example request
sections.body: GET /example/v1/entries/entry_001 returns an entry when the caller has access. Example response: {"id":"entry_001","title":"Approved menu","status":"draft","owner_label":"Café owner"}.

sections.title: Errors and consistency
sections.body: Document 401 for missing authentication, 403 for insufficient access, and 404 for an unavailable resource according to the actual service’s disclosure policy. Describe retry behavior and concurrency rules rather than leaving clients to guess.

sections.title: Before implementation
sections.body: Replace this proposed contract with the reviewed schema, real authentication flow, and tested examples. Keep tokens out of documentation and verify each example against the actual API version.

questions: actual API version, resources, schema, authentication, permissions, errors, pagination and verified examples

title: Release Notes
headline: What changed, and what you need to do.
description: Release notes organized by user-visible changes, fixes, known issues, and upgrade actions.
context: This fictional release describes a handover library update. Version 0.4 is an example release identifier and does not represent a Claw Me production release.

sections.title: What to try
sections.body: Open a handover index, check the owner label, and review an entry with a long title on mobile. The release should make those everyday tasks clearer.

sections.title: Action for existing entries
sections.body: Review older entries and add a date when their content has actually been checked. Do not populate a fictional review date merely to make the list look complete.

sections.title: Release evidence
sections.body: In a real release note, link the verified version, migration instructions, and support route. Describe only changes that shipped, keeping planned work in the roadmap.

questions: verified release version and date, shipped changes, fixes, known issues, migration actions and support links

title: Roadmap Snapshot
headline: Show the sequence without pretending every date is fixed.
description: A roadmap snapshot with now/next/later work, outcomes, dependencies, and confidence.
context: This fictional handover product roadmap is a planning snapshot. The horizons express order and uncertainty; they are not public delivery commitments.
rows: Receiving teams know who updates an item

sections.title: Why this order
sections.body: Ownership addresses the immediate handover problem. Reminder behavior depends on a meaningful review date. Bulk import is useful only if larger libraries are a verified need.

sections.title: What can change
sections.body: Research, delivery effort, and operational constraints may change the sequence. Record the reason for a change rather than silently moving an item between horizons.

sections.title: Review the roadmap
sections.body: At the next planning review, compare each item with evidence and capacity. Keep committed work distinct from exploratory ideas so the audience understands the confidence behind the plan.

questions: planning horizon, outcomes, initiatives, dependencies, confidence, commitments and review cadence

title: Architecture Decision
headline: Record the choice future maintainers will question.
description: An architecture decision record with context, alternatives, consequences, and revisit conditions.
context: This fictional decision considers how to render a small handover library. It proposes static HTML for a read-mostly reference surface, subject to the actual application’s requirements.

sections.title: Context and decision
sections.body: The first use case is reading a small number of approved handover pages. The team chooses static HTML for the initial reference surface because custom operational actions are outside the first scope.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.body: The publishing process must bundle assets and preserve accessibility. Content updates need an owner and a repeatable build. The decision does not remove the need for the actual platform’s access controls.

sections.title: Revisit when
sections.body: Reconsider if frequent multi-author editing becomes a verified requirement or if the reference surface must perform stateful operations. Link the evidence and the superseding decision rather than rewriting history.

questions: technical context, requirements, alternatives, verified constraints, decision, consequences and revisit triggers

title: QA Test Plan
headline: Test the task that matters to the user.
description: A QA plan with realistic scenarios, expected results, evidence, and release criteria.
context: This fictional test plan covers a handover index on desktop and mobile. It prioritizes finding the correct item, understanding its status, and using its links.
rows: Every link and disclosure is reachable

sections.title: Test setup
sections.body: Use a controlled example with draft, approved, and archived entries. Include a long title and a missing reference case. Record the browser, viewport, version, and source data.

sections.title: Failure handling
sections.body: Describe the expected and actual result with a minimal reproduction. Keep the severity tied to the user’s task and record a named owner for the next action.

sections.title: Exit criteria
sections.body: The critical lookup and reference-opening tasks pass, keyboard operation works, and known limitations are reviewed by the release owner. Do not equate a screenshot with complete functional coverage.

questions: release scope, critical user tasks, environments, fixtures, expected results, evidence and exit criteria

title: Accessibility Review
headline: Make the finding specific enough to fix.
description: An accessibility review worksheet with observed barriers, affected tasks, and verification steps.
context: This fictional review illustrates findings on a document index. It is a sample review record, not a certification of conformance or a claim about a live site.

sections.title: Describe the barrier
sections.body: A useful finding explains what the person is trying to do and how the interface prevents or complicates it. Attach a concrete example rather than a vague instruction to improve accessibility.

sections.title: Check the repair
sections.body: Repeat the affected task after the change. Combine automated checks with keyboard review and appropriate assistive-technology testing; no single tool establishes complete accessibility.

sections.title: Keep the scope visible
sections.body: Record the pages, components, environments, and methods actually reviewed. In a formal assessment, map findings to the current applicable standard using verified references.

questions: review scope, users and tasks, observed findings, test methods, applicable standard, owners and verification

title: Developer Onboarding
headline: Reach a working example before changing the system.
description: A developer onboarding guide with repository orientation, setup checks, and a first contribution.

sections.title: A useful repository map
sections.body: Start with the README, contributor agreement, template catalog, shared styles, and build script. Identify which files are canonical and which are generated before editing either.

sections.title: First contribution
sections.body: Improve one unclear label or a small content example. Build the artifact, check desktop and mobile output, and explain the user-visible change in the review description.

sections.title: When setup fails
sections.body: Record the command, expected result, actual error, and relevant runtime version. Keep secrets out of logs and ask the responsible maintainer about missing access rather than inventing configuration values.

questions: repository, supported runtimes, verified setup commands, architecture map, access needs, tests and contribution workflow
